name: Low Earth Orbit 550 km
tooltip: A low, tilted orbit. A satellite at 550 km makes about 15 orbits a day and sees sharp detail, but spends about a third of each orbit in Earth's shadow and slowly loses altitude to air drag. Tilted 53 degrees, it never passes over the polar regions.
source: period, eclipse, contact: GMAT R2026a run (leo_550_events.script, ground station at 40 N, 4 W as a placeholder, 10 degree minimum elevation); inclination 53: assumption; revisit, life, delta-v: estimate

name: Sun-synchronous orbit 700 km
tooltip: A near-polar orbit that crosses the equator at the same local time every day, so lighting is consistent from one image to the next. It covers the whole globe, including the poles, but it is higher and the satellite is in shadow about a third of each orbit.
source: period, eclipse, contact: GMAT R2026a run (sso_700_events.script, first partial eclipse excluded, same placeholder station); altitude and inclination: data brief; revisit, life, delta-v: estimate

name: Lunar polar orbit 50 km
tooltip: A low polar orbit around the Moon passes over every part of the surface as the Moon rotates beneath it. Reaching it needs a braking burn of roughly 700 m/s, and about four days of travel from Earth. The orbit is unstable and needs regular corrections.
source: period: calculated from lunar radius 1,737 km plus 50 km and the Moon's gravitational parameter 4,902.8 km3/s2; eclipse: calculated geometric maximum (Sun in the orbit plane); contact: game value (not simulated); revisit: the Moon's rotation period of 27.3 days; delta-v: estimate (550 to 800 m/s plausible; brief's NASA study range 517 to 731 m/s); transfer time about 4 days (LRO: https://www.lroc.asu.edu/assets/LROC_instrument_overview-5b07a1035bc2625c486e7f3d5777034224aa9b6ea887b61fcfd962f863c675f9.pdf)
